The on-chip invisibility cloak is realized by confining electromagnetic fields in a three-dimensional array of over 5,000 waveguides fabricated using femtosecond laser direct writing.
The hidden object that can be concealed by the cloak has dimensions of 0.44mm x 0.35mm.
The optimal pitch between the waveguides was found to be 21 μm, providing the best image transfer quality.
The cloak exhibits a tolerance for viewing angle of 8.0° laterally and 6.7° vertically, beyond which the inner structure becomes visible.
Tomography analysis was used to visualize the evolution of the light field as it propagates through the cloaking structure.
The normalized cross-correlation metric was used to quantitatively evaluate the similarity between the input and output images, reaching a peak value of 0.986 at the 21 μm pitch.
The background noise level, as measured by the cross-correlation of the regions outside the target image, was found to be around 0.18 ± 0.03.
The cloaking approach can be extended to three dimensions by increasing the complexity of the waveguide arrangement and number of printed waveguides.
The printed cloak enables novel applications in integrated photonics, such as concealing coupling or swapping operations from external observation.
Key challenges include mitigating phase distortion from waveguide length differences and further increasing the cloaked volume by optimizing the waveguide curvature and density.
The cloaking is achieved by guiding light around the hidden object through the three-dimensional waveguide array, rather than using transformation optics or carpet cloaking approaches.
The femtosecond laser direct writing technique allows for the fabrication of complex three-dimensional waveguide structures on the photonic chip.
The authors demonstrate the first experimental realization of an invisibility cloak printed directly on a photonic chip.
The cloaking performance was characterized through various analyses, including normalized cross-correlation, tomography, and viewing angle scans.
The on-chip cloak can conceal millimeter-scale structures while maintaining high-quality image transfer through the waveguide array.
